title: 20 EMA Pullback
teaches: The 20 EMA pullback as we trade it: a leader in a rising trend, above its 200-day with the 20 EMA over a rising 50-day, drifts quietly back to the rising 20 EMA, a session holds the line, the buy is a cent over that session's high at market in regular hours, the stop sits a few cents under its low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: the odds are very high that when a security makes a new momentum high and pulls back, it will retest its recent high. Therefore, any pullback from a new momentum high can be bought.
facts.claim: Raschke on the Holy Grail: after a new momentum high the odds are very high a pullback retests the recent high, so any such pullback can be bought.

facts.quote: 2. Look for a retracement in price to the 20 period exponential moving average. This will usually be accompanied by a turndown in the ADX.
facts.claim: Raschke's rule: look for a retracement to the 20-period exponential moving average.

facts.quote: 3. When the price touches the 20 period moving average, put a buy stop above the high of the previous bar.
facts.claim: Raschke's buy: a buy stop above the high of the previous bar once price touches the 20-period average.

facts.quote: 4. Once filled, enter a protective sell stop at the newly formed swing low. Trail stops as profits grow.
facts.claim: Raschke's stop: the newly formed swing low, trailed as profits grow.

facts.quote: This is a case where there is no reason to be in this trade.
facts.claim: Raschke on a pullback buy that showed little movement for five days: no reason to be in the trade.

facts.quote: On the 30-minute time frame, the ADX rose above 30, so we’ll buy the first retrace-ment to the 20-period EMA and look to exit on a push to new highs.
facts.claim: Raschke buys the first retracement to the 20-period EMA after a strong trend.

facts.quote: I use market orders most of the time.
facts.claim: Raschke uses market orders most of the time.

facts.quote: By focusing on the 10 and 20-day exponential moving averages (EMAs), you can identify key moments to buy stocks when the price dips into these levels after a strong rally.
facts.claim: Kell: buy the dip into the 10 and 20-day EMAs after a strong rally.

facts.quote: But always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in before making your trade.
facts.claim: Kell: always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in.

facts.quote: The EMA Crossback refers to the first time the stock price retests its moving averages after a strong upward move, called a “Wedge Pop.”
facts.claim: Kell: the EMA Crossback is the first retest of the averages after a Wedge Pop.

facts.quote: The EMA Crossback works best when the price gently moves sideways, allowing the moving averages to rise to the price.
facts.claim: Kell: the pullback works best when price drifts sideways and the rising averages catch up.

facts.quote: During the consolidation the stock price “surfs” the rising 10- and 20-day. and sometimes toe 50-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a leader surfs its rising 10 and 20-day lines and sometimes toes the 50-day.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day, no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: A big move higher sometime in the past 1-3 months. This move can be anywhere from 30-100%+ and usually lasts a few days to a few weeks.
facts.claim: Kullamagi wants a big move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months first.

facts.quote: If a beginner stick to the 10-day. You wait for the first CLOSE below the 10- day.
facts.claim: Kullamagi trails the 10-day and sells on the first close below it.

facts.quote: As long as the price remains above the 21-day EMA, any short-term movements can be considered noise, rather than a clear signal of a change in trend.
facts.claim: Keller: above the 21-day EMA, short-term moves are noise, not a change of trend.

facts.quote: The price is above the 21-day EMA, the 21-day is above the 50-day SMA, and the 50-day is above the 200-day SMA.
facts.claim: Keller's proper order: price over the 21-day EMA, over the 50-day, over the 200-day.

facts.quote: I think of the 21-day EMA as the first line of defense, an initial stop within an uptrend phase.
facts.claim: Keller calls the 21-day EMA the first line of defense in an uptrend.

facts.quote: chasing stocks hitting a new high in price can be the surest way to frustration

facts.quote: a moving average gives you a reason to study price action closely as it approaches, not a reason to act automatically.

walkthroughs.title: GE, January 2024: the low kisses the line
steps: GE, January 2024. A leader in a rising trend drifts four days back to its rising 20 EMA on 0.78x volume.
The hold session: the low kisses the line to the cent and closes above it. Above the 50-day and 200-day.
Next session trades a cent over the hold candle's high. Buy at market, 100.39. Stop a few cents under its low, 99.07.
Failure mode: a slice back through the line that takes the day's low. Instead, 3R in 5 sessions. Time to sell part.

walkthroughs.title: NVDA, May 2023: the textbook leader, out before the report
steps: NVDA, May 2023. A rising line, a light-volume four-day rest, 1.4 ATR off the high, pullback volume 0.74x.
The hold session closes above the line. Buy a cent over its high at market, 28.79. Stop under its low, 28.02.
3R in 3 sessions: a fair first sell, stop to breakeven. It stood at 3.9R the day before the report.
Hold through a report only if up 5R. We are out before the gap. The rule costs one gap and saves many.

walkthroughs.title: CRM, June 2020: the shallow shakeout
steps: CRM, June 2020. A four-day pullback, 2.4 ATR off the high on 0.76x volume. The low dips 0.28 ATR under the line.
The same session closes back above the 20 EMA. That is a shakeout, not a lost line. The hold is in.
Next session trades a cent over the hold candle's high. Buy at market, 183.72. Stop a few cents under its low, 179.97.
Failure mode: a second close under the line before the trigger. Instead, 3R in 2 sessions. We hold.

questions.q: In one line, what is a 20 EMA pullback?
choices: A leader resting on its rising 20 EMA
A stock sliding below a falling 20 EMA
A tight box under a flat ceiling
A sharp V-bottom off the 200-day
questions.answer: A leader resting on its rising 20 EMA
questions.why: A leader resting on its rising 20 EMA. In a rising trend that line is a level many traders watch, so buyers tend to step in there. That lets us put a small stop just under the day's low. Keller calls the 21-day EMA the first line of defense in an uptrend. Kullamagi has a leader surf its rising 10 and 20-day lines.
questions.lesson_line: A pullback is a leader catching its breath at a line that is still rising.

wrong.A tight box under a flat ceiling: That is a flat base. A pullback is a dip to a moving line, not a rest under a level.
wrong.A sharp V-bottom off the 200-day: A pullback sits in a rising trend above the 200-day. A V-bottom is a reversal.
wrong.A stock sliding below a falling 20 EMA: That is a downtrend. A pullback needs a leader and a 20 EMA that is still rising.

questions.simple: A strong stock rests at a rising 20 EMA, where buyers tend to step in, so our stop can be small.

deeper.example: GE, January 2024: four days back to its 20 EMA on 0.78x volume. The low kissed the line to the cent. That is the shape of the setup.

reasons: card numbers are proposed, not rulings
several facts agree

questions.story: The chart ends on the day a session holds the line.

questions.q: Which line must the hold session close above, by our hard rule?
choices: The 200-day simple average
The 50-day SMA, if it is rising
The 9 EMA, closing back over it
No line; the touch is enough
questions.why: The 200-day simple average. We take no longs below it, unless it is a parabolic long. Above it the larger trend is innocent until proven guilty, so a dip is more likely a rest than a reversal. Below it the stock is in a downtrend, and a pullback there is really a bounce.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day there is no pullback to buy, only a bounce.

wrong.The 50-day SMA, if it is rising: The 50-day matters for the stack of averages, but the hard rule is the 200-day.
wrong.The 9 EMA, closing back over it: A close back over the 9 EMA is a confirming sign, not a requirement.
wrong.No line; the touch is enough: The touch is the pattern. The 200-day comes first: we take no longs below it.

questions.simple: The 200-day line, because above it the big trend is up and a dip is more likely a rest than a reversal.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B26

questions.story: The chart ends on the hold session.

questions.q: On a 20 EMA pullback the stop goes a few cents under the low of the session that held the line.
questions.why: True. The stop goes a few cents under the low of the hold session, not exactly on it. If price trades under that low, the hold has failed, so we are out with a small loss. The few cents keep an ordinary tick to the low from stopping us. Kullamagi also sets the stop at the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the hold session's low.
questions.simple: True, because a trade under the hold session's low means the hold failed, so we leave there with a small loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and F62

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The 20 EMA must be ___: higher than it was 10 sessions earlier.
questions.why: Rising. The 20 EMA must be higher than it was 10 sessions earlier. A line that flattens or turns down before entry ends the setup. Kell: the pullback works best when the rising averages catch up to the price.
questions.lesson_line: A rising line is the whole setup. A flat one is a different chart.
questions.simple: The line must be higher than it was 10 sessions ago, so the stock rests on a line that still climbs.

reasons: the 10-session test is a proposed card number

questions.q: A session held the 20 EMA and closed above it. Where is the buy we draw on the chart?
choices: A cent over the hold candle's high
At the close of the hold session
A limit order resting on the 20 EMA
A close back over the 9 EMA
questions.answer: A cent over the hold candle's high
questions.why: A cent over the hold candle's high, bought at market on a later session. Trading over that high shows buyers pushing past the session that held, which is the confirmation Kell asks for. The close only shows the hold. A limit order on the line buys before anything has held.
questions.lesson_line: The hold candle sets the trigger. Over its high, we are in.

wrong.At the close of the hold session: The close is the hold itself, not the buy. Our buy waits for price to trade over the hold candle's high on a later session.
wrong.A limit order resting on the 20 EMA: That buys before anything has held. Never buy before a session holds the line.
wrong.A close back over the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA remount is a confirming sign in grading, not the trigger.

questions.simple: We buy once price trades a cent over the hold candle's high, because that is when buyers show they are pushing it up.

deeper.trap: Buying the touch itself, before any session has held, is a named mistake. Kell: always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in. The hold candle's high is a level to set an alert on, and the buy happens only when it trades.

reasons: the cent-over-the-high buy is the proposed fallback trigger, held under D-003

questions.story: The chart ends on the hold session. Our buy is drawn for the next session.

questions.q: Entries on a 20 EMA pullback are limit orders placed on the 20 EMA, in regular hours only.
questions.why: False. Entries are market orders, not limit orders resting on the 20 EMA. We buy in regular trading hours only, with no new buys outside them. Raschke is one voice on this: I use market orders most of the time.
questions.lesson_line: Market order the moment it trades. Regular hours only.
questions.simple: False, because we enter with market orders in regular hours, not limit orders resting on the line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E57 and E58

questions.q: If the trend is strong enough, you may buy the first touch of the 20 EMA before any session has held it.
questions.why: False. A moving average is not a wall, and stocks run through the line all the time. A touch only shows price arrived. A session that holds the line is the proof buyers showed up, so we wait for it, even if it costs a little price. Shannon: a moving average is a reason to watch price closely, not a reason to act automatically.
questions.lesson_line: The line is a place to watch, not a reason to act. Let a session hold it first.
questions.simple: False, because a touch only shows price arrived, so we wait for a session to hold the line and show buyers.

reasons: the never-before-hold rule is a proposed card line
if D-003 moves the buy to the hold session itself, the wording may need a re-read

questions.q: During the pullback the session's low reaches under the 50-day SMA. Which card is it now, if anything?
choices: The 50-day MA pullback
Still the 20 EMA pullback
A Remount of the 50-day
A bull flag on the 50-day
questions.why: The 50-day form of the moving-average pullback, if anything. The 20 EMA pullback needs the hold session's low to stay above the 50-day SMA. Once the low reaches the 50-day, the 50-day is the line, and it is judged on its own card.
questions.lesson_line: Name the line the low touched. The 50-day is a different card.

wrong.Still the 20 EMA pullback: The 20 EMA pullback's low holds above the 50-day. This low went through it.
wrong.A Remount of the 50-day: A Remount is a line lost and retaken, not a dip. One session's low under the 50-day is not that.
wrong.A bull flag on the 50-day: A flag needs a pole. The question here is only which line the low touched.

questions.simple: The 50-day pullback, because the low went down to the 50-day, so that is the line that was tested.

reasons: the 50-day boundary is a proposed card line
fixed before

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On our card, the pullback lasts 2 to ___ sessions from the swing high to the hold session.
questions.why: 15. The card says the pullback lasts 2 to 15 sessions from the swing high to the hold session. Our examples ran 4 to 10 sessions, such as TOL's 10-day drift. A drift past 15 sessions does not fit this card.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions: two to fifteen on our card.
questions.simple: On our card a pullback may last at most 15 sessions, counted from the swing high to the hold session.

deeper.example: TOL in 2004 drifted 10 days down to the line on 0.69x volume and reached 3R in 6 sessions. GE took only 4 days. Both fit the 2 to 15 session window, so the cap is a limit, not a target.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c04)
the 2 to 15 length is a proposed number that may change; other dossiers say 2 to 8 and 2 to 10
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Read the red days and the volume bars on the way down. What makes this pullback grade well?
choices: Small red days and volume drying up
A few big red days on rising volume
One huge red day to the line
A gap down through the 50-day
questions.answer: Small red days and volume drying up
questions.why: Small red days with volume drying up. Little selling means holders are staying, so the line is more likely to hold. TraderLion calls a slow drift into the EMAs ideal. A heavy-volume down day is a warning and a lower grade, not a veto. A lower grade can mean a smaller size.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet drift of small bars grades best. A heavy red day is a warning and a lower grade, not a veto.

wrong.One huge red day to the line: One huge red day is a sell-off, not a quiet rest. It points to sellers in control.
wrong.A few big red days on rising volume: Big red days on rising volume are sellers pressing. A heavy-volume down day lowers the grade, though it does not end the setup.
wrong.A gap down through the 50-day: That breaks the 50-day. It is no longer a 20 EMA pullback.

questions.simple: Small red days on volume that dries up mean little selling, so the line is more likely to hold.

reasons: rests on the settled HEAVY-DOWN ruling (2026-11-14)
the 1.5x line is a card number

questions.story: A leader has drifted six days back to its rising 20 EMA. The chart ends on the day a session holds the line. Our grade (A+, A, B, B-) is our judgment of how clean a setup is, and it sets the size.

questions.q: A stock drifting along its 20 EMA, no swing high at least 1 ATR above the hold low, has not pulled back.
questions.why: True. The card needs the pullback to be at least 1 ATR off the swing high. That is measured from the highest high of the last 11 sessions to the hold session's low. A stock sliding along the line with no such dip has nothing to pull back from.
questions.lesson_line: You need something to pull back from. Measure the dip in ATR.
questions.simple: True, because the card needs a dip of at least 1 ATR from the swing high before it counts as a pullback.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c03)
the 1 ATR depth and the 11 session window are proposed numbers
tied to held decision D-029
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Which low counts as a touch by the card?
choices: Low of 51.00
A low of 48.30
Low of 47.90
Low of 46.00
questions.why: A low of 48.30. The touch band runs from 0.25 ATR above the 20 EMA to 1 ATR below it. With an ATR of 2.00, 48.30 is under the line by less than one ATR. The line gets run through; it is not a wall.
questions.lesson_line: A touch has a band: a little above the line, up to one ATR under it.

wrong.Low of 51.00: That low stayed more than 0.25 ATR above the line. It never came down to touch it.
wrong.Low of 47.90: That is under the line by more than one ATR of 2.00. It went through the touch band, not into it.
wrong.Low of 46.00: That is far more than one ATR under the line. The line gets run through, but not by that much.

questions.story: Four stocks each have a 20 EMA at 50.00 and an ATR of 2.00. Each closes above the line today, but their lows differ.
questions.simple: A low of 48.30, because it is under the line by less than one ATR, which is inside the touch band.

reasons: the touch band is a proposed card number
key rests on a comparison

questions.q: If the pullback keeps closing under the 20 EMA, the line is lost and the setup is off.
questions.why: True. Closes that keep sitting under the 20 EMA mean the line is lost. The setup is off until it sets up again. One shakeout that is reclaimed the next session can still be a hold. How deep a dip may go, and how fast it must come back, is a judgment call, not a fixed number.
questions.lesson_line: One shakeout can be fine. Closes that stay under the line mean it is lost.
questions.simple: True, because closes that stay under the 20 EMA mean the line is lost, and we wait for a new setup.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c14)
the two closes and 0.5 ATR lines are proposed numbers
tied to held decision D-036
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: A scanner puts the stop at the line minus 1 ATR. Why is that not our stop?
choices: Too wide; use the day's low
Too wide only for slow movers
Too tight; it sits inside the noise
Too tight; use the 50-day instead
questions.answer: Too wide; use the day's low
questions.why: Too wide. The line minus 1 ATR is wider than 1 ATR whenever the entry is above the line. Our stop is a few cents under the hold session's low, and it is a real order with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is a price under a candle, not a line minus a cushion.

wrong.Too tight; it sits inside the noise: It is the other way round: a cushion under the line is wider than the day's low, not tighter.
wrong.Too wide only for slow movers: The line minus 1 ATR is wider than 1 ATR whenever the entry is above the line, for any mover.
wrong.Too tight; use the 50-day instead: The line minus 1 ATR is wider, not tighter. And our stop is not the 50-day: it is a price a few cents under the hold session's low.

questions.simple: It is too wide, because our stop goes just under the low of the hold session instead.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and F62

questions.q: Your initial stop can be a close under the 20 EMA that you watch for, as long as you act on it.
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. A close under a line cannot sit with the broker as an order, so it cannot be the initial stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: False, because a stop must be a real order with the broker and a close under a line cannot be one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D41

questions.q: On the hold session, where should the 20 EMA sit against the 50-day SMA?
choices: Above a rising 50-day SMA
Above a falling 50-day SMA
Below the 50-day, catching up
Crossing it that session
questions.why: Above a 50-day SMA that is itself climbing. The short average leading the medium one means the trend is up at both speeds, so this is a leader resting, not a stock in repair. Keller's proper order stacks price over the fast EMA, the fast EMA over the 50-day, and the 50-day over the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Stacked and rising: the 20 EMA over a rising 50-day. Then look at the dip.

wrong.Below the 50-day, catching up: A 20 EMA under the 50-day is a stock in repair, not a leader resting.
wrong.Crossing it that session: A cross is the line changing sides. We want the order already settled.
wrong.Above a falling 50-day SMA: A falling 50-day means the medium trend is not up. We want it climbing under the 20 EMA.

questions.simple: The 20 EMA over a climbing 50-day shows the trend is up at both speeds, so the stock is resting, not in repair.

reasons: the 20-over-50 order is a proposed card line, not the owner's B26

questions.story: The hold session. Read the two averages on the chart.

questions.q: Is this a good 20 EMA pullback to buy?
choices: No; the line has stopped rising
Yes; the touch itself is what counts
Yes; a late tap is the strongest tap
Yes; four months up proves the trend
questions.answer: No; the line has stopped rising
questions.why: No. A pullback buys a leader resting at a line that is still climbing. Once the line goes flat, the trend that carried the stock has tired, so the tap has little to bounce from.
questions.lesson_line: A tired line does not hold. Pass the tap of a flattening 20 EMA.

wrong.Yes; the touch itself is what counts: The touch is only the pattern. The line must still be rising first.
wrong.Yes; a late tap is the strongest tap: A tap of a line that has gone flat is no stronger. The trend behind it has tired.
wrong.Yes; four months up proves the trend: A past run is not support. The line has stopped rising, so little lift is left to hold the tap.

questions.story: A leader has run four months. Its 20 EMA has stopped rising and gone flat, and price drifts down into it. Today it taps the line.
questions.simple: No, because a flat line means the trend has tired, so the tap has little to bounce from.

reasons: the flat-line test is a proposed card number

questions.q: Buy the hold?
choices: No; the report is inside 3 days
Yes; a first tap is best
Yes; but at half size
No; it needs a second session
questions.answer: No; the report is inside 3 days
questions.why: No. We take no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. This one reports in two days, so a buy tomorrow sits inside that window. A report can gap the stock right through the stop, and a stop cannot catch an overnight gap. The 5R exception is for holding a trade already open, not for a new buy. If the stock still sets up after the report, it can hold again.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before a report. Wait, then look again.

wrong.Yes; a first tap is best: The tap is fine, but the rulebook bars new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.Yes; but at half size: Size does not change the rule. A smaller buy is still a new buy inside the window.
wrong.No; it needs a second session: One session that holds the line is enough. The reason to pass is the report inside the window.

questions.story: A leader's first tap of its rising 20 EMA holds today and closes above the line. The company reports in two days, after the close.
questions.simple: No, because earnings can gap the stock past our stop overnight, so we wait until the report is out.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h08)
rests on the owner's rulebook B22; whether the 3 days are sessions or calendar days is held under D-072

questions.q: Bought the hold at 147.30 with the stop at 145.05. Where is 3R?
questions.why: One R is the fill minus the stop, 147.30 minus 145.05. Add three of those to the fill: 147.30 plus 3 times (147.30 minus 145.05) is 154.05. 3R is a yardstick, not a fixed sale point.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a yardstick, and the first sell is a judgment.
questions.simple: 3R sits at 154.05, which is the fill plus three times the stop distance.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h05)
computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook B19

wrong.$149.55: That adds one R, not three.
wrong.$151.80: That counts 3R up from the stop, not from the fill.
wrong.$156.30: That adds four R. Three R is three gaps, not four.

questions.q: By our default, which line does the rest of a winner trail?
choices: The 9 EMA or the 20 EMA
The 50-day or 200-day line
The prior day's low, daily
No trail; sell it all at 5R
questions.why: The 9 EMA for a fast mover, the 20 EMA for a steadier one, sold on a close below it. A close under the rising average is the first sign the move that paid us has turned, so what is left is sold before the gain fades. Kullamagi's own trail is the first close below his 10-day. The first sells are a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the rising average. Sell the close below it, not the touch.

wrong.The 50-day or 200-day line: Our default trail is the 9 EMA or the 20 EMA, not these.
wrong.The prior day's low, daily: Our default trails an average and sells on a close below it, not a daily low.
wrong.No trail; sell it all at 5R: 5R is not a fixed exit. What is left rides the trail.

questions.simple: We sell what is left on a close under the 9 or 20 EMA, because that first shows the move has turned.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h21)
rests on the owner's rulebook E52; trail timing is held under D-024
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: We buy this pullback in leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups.
questions.why: True. We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. An RS rating ranks a stock's strength against the rest of the market. A dip in a leader is a rest in a rising trend, while a dip in a laggard is often a bounce in a downtrend. Bonde: buying pullbacks in most small caps would make you a bag holder.
questions.lesson_line: A pullback in a laggard is a dip in a downtrend. Buy the leaders.
questions.simple: True, because a dip in a leader is a rest in an uptrend, while a dip in a laggard can keep falling.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C31
Bonde's quote is about small caps

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A down day into the line on more than ___ times the 50-day volume is a distribution day to be mindful of.
questions.why: 1.5. A down day into the line on more than 1.5 times the 50-day volume is a distribution day to be mindful of. It is a warning and a lower grade, not an invalidation. Shannon looks for volume contracting during pullbacks.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet into the line is a rest. Loud into the line is a warning and a lower grade.
questions.simple: It is 1.5 times the 50-day average volume. A down day above that is a warning and lowers the grade.

reasons: rests on the settled HEAVY-DOWN ruling (2026-11-14)
the 1.5x line is a card number

questions.q: What is true of your trade now?
choices: Stopped out; the loss is booked
Still in; it closed above 59.17
Stopped out; a re-buy needs no trigger
Still in; stops only count on closes
questions.answer: Stopped out; the loss is booked
questions.why: Stopped out. The stop is the exit, and the day's low of 58.57 traded through the stop at 59.17. The later close at 59.21 does not undo that. We set the stop so the loss is small and known before the trade, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working. GILD did this and went on without us.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at the stop is the system working, not a mistake.

wrong.Still in; it closed above 59.17: The stop order fired when the low traded through it. A later close above the stop does not undo that.
wrong.Stopped out; a re-buy needs no trigger: After a stop-out we buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade. A bounce is not a trigger.
wrong.Still in; stops only count on closes: A stop order fires when price trades through it. It does not wait for a close.

questions.story: You bought the hold at 60.50 with the stop at 59.17. Next day the stock trades down through the stop, the low prints 58.57, and it closes back at 59.21.
questions.simple: You were stopped out, because the low traded through the stop. The loss was planned and small, so taking it is the system working.

deeper.example: GILD in 2013: bought at 60.50 with the stop at 59.17. Next day the low hit 58.57 and the stop fired, then it closed back at 59.21. It reached the 3R level (64.49) on 09-18 and 5R (67.15) on 10-17 without us. The loss was still the plan working.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A4 and B21
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Ten trading days after the buy the trade sits at 0.6R, doing nothing. Our rule?
choices: Sell it and free up the money
Hold; the stop will do the exiting
Add another third at a higher price
Move the stop up to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it and free up the money
questions.why: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. R is the amount risked on the trade, so 0.6R is a small gain for ten days of waiting. That money can go into a setup that is working. Raschke on a pullback buy that went nowhere: there is no reason to be in this trade.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.

wrong.Hold; the stop will do the exiting: The stop is one exit. The time stop is the other, and ten days have passed.
wrong.Add another third at a higher price: No adding, and nothing is working. The rule frees the money.
wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R. At 0.6R the time stop applies.

questions.simple: Sell, because a trade that has done nothing in 10 days ties up money a better setup could use.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C33

questions.q: The highest high of the last 11 sessions is 120.00, ATR is 3.00 and the hold session's low is 117.60. How deep is the pullback, in ATR?
questions.why: The pullback is the swing high minus the hold low, divided by the ATR: (120.00 minus 117.60) divided by 3.00 is 0.8. The card wants at least 1 ATR, so this is a drift along the line, not a pullback to it.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the dip in ATR. Under one, there was nothing to pull back from.
questions.simple: The dip is 0.8 ATR, which is under the 1 ATR the card needs, so it is not a pullback.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c03)
computed key on a proposed 1 ATR number
tied to held decision D-029

choices: 0.08 ATR
2.40 ATR
1.25 ATR
0.80 ATR

wrong.1.25 ATR: That flips the division. Put the dip on top.
wrong.2.40 ATR: That is the dollar dip read as ATR. Divide it by the ATR.

questions.q: Fill 48.60. The hold candle's low is 47.45 and the stop sits three cents under it. Stop distance below the fill, in percent, to 2 decimals?
questions.why: The stop is three cents under the 47.45 low, so it sits at 47.45 minus 0.03. Divide the gap from the fill by the fill: (48.60 minus (47.45 minus 0.03)) divided by 48.60 is 2.43%. That is inside the about 3% a stop usually stays within.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: The stop sits about 2.43% below the fill: a few cents under the low, divided by the fill.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook F62 and A13

wrong.1.18%: That is the dollar amount read as a percent. Divide it first.
wrong.97.6%: That is the stop as a share of the fill, not the gap.

questions.q: Account 40,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 95.90, stop 93.85. Shares from the risk math, rounded down?
questions.why: Risk is 0.5% of the 40,000 account, which is 200. Divide that by the stop distance, 95.90 minus 93.85, and round down to 97. Sizing from the stop means a stop-out costs about 200 whatever the stop distance, so the loss is the one we planned. The size is the smaller of this and the position cap.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. You never pick a size and back-fit a stop.
questions.simple: We buy 97 shares, because the size comes from the stop, so a stop-out costs only the 0.5% we planned.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook A5
fixed before by the checker

choices: 200 shares
975 shares
97 shares
2 shares

wrong.975 shares: That risks ten times the plan. A decimal slip.
wrong.2 shares: That divides the dollar risk by the price, not by the stop distance.
wrong.200 shares: That is the risk dollars read as shares. Divide by the risk per share.

questions.story: Bought at the trigger.

questions.q: Buy the open?
choices: No; over 4% past the trigger
No; a gap up voids the hold
Yes; the gap shows strength
Yes; the stop caps the risk anyway
questions.why: No. The open at 52.40 is more than 4% over the 50.00 hold high. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the hold candle, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. A morning flush that curls back up is one way in.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the trigger and we are done. We would rather miss it than chase it.

wrong.Yes; the gap shows strength: Strength and too far away are both true. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.No; a gap up voids the hold: A gap up does not void the hold. A fill not more than 4% over the trigger is still allowed.
wrong.Yes; the stop caps the risk anyway: A stop caps the loss, not the chase. The rule is never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and the stretch costs you shares.

questions.story: The hold candle's high is 50.00. Next morning the stock gaps open at 52.40 and keeps going.
questions.simple: No, because chasing leaves the stop far below the price, so we could buy only a small size.

deeper.counter: A gap is not always a chase. A fill not more than 4% above the trigger is allowed. The stop stays put under the hold candle, so the shares shrink.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook C28
a computed gap

questions.q: What do you do the moment it trades a cent over the high?
choices: Buy now; stop under the hold low
Wait for the day's close to confirm
Place a limit order on the 20 EMA
Go in now; stop on the 20 EMA line
questions.answer: Buy now; stop under the hold low
questions.why: Buy at market as it trades a cent over the hold candle's high. That move shows buyers pushing past the session that held, and the stop under the hold low keeps the risk small. The stop sits a few cents under the hold candle's low, or under today's low if that is lower. Waiting for the close would mean paying more for the same stop.
questions.lesson_line: Alert at the hold candle's high. When it trades, you buy; you do not wait for the bell.

wrong.Place a limit order on the 20 EMA: Our entries are market orders. A limit on the line sits below the market and may never fill.
wrong.Wait for the day's close to confirm: The trigger is the trade through the hold candle's high, not the close. It has already fired.
wrong.Go in now; stop on the 20 EMA line: The stop is a few cents under the candle's low, not on a line. A stop sitting right on a line is easy to hit.

questions.story: The hold session. The next morning it opens flat, stays above that session's low, then trades a cent over that session's high.
questions.simple: Buy now, because the trade over the hold high is the signal, and waiting for the close costs a worse price.

reasons: teaches the proposed fallback trigger, held under D-003
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Is this the 20 EMA pullback?
choices: No; the low reached the 50-day
Yes; the 20 EMA was tagged too
Yes; both lines held the close
questions.why: No. The hold session's low must hold above the 50-day. This low sat under 408.58, so it is the 50-day form of the moving-average pullback, if anything. HD did this and stopped.
questions.lesson_line: When the low reaches the 50-day, the 50-day is the line. Judge it on that card.

wrong.Yes; the 20 EMA was tagged too: The 20 EMA was on the way down. The low went through it to the 50-day.
wrong.Yes; both lines held the close: The close is not the test here. The low broke the 50-day, which ends the 20 EMA card.

questions.story: The pullback low prints 401.01. The 50-day SMA sits at 408.58 and the 20 EMA at 408.60.

questions.q: A 20 EMA pullback can be an add-on to a position you already hold, at the same stop.
questions.why: False. The 20 EMA pullback is a new trade at full size, at one price with one stop. We do not add or start small. One stop on one buy fixes the risk before the trade, and an add would give the position a second price and blur it.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, full size. The pullback is a trade, not a top-up.
questions.simple: False, because each buy is one trade with one stop, so the risk is known before we start.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A5

questions.q: What is the stop now?
choices: 96.10, the first 30-minute low
Sell at the open, 96.50
No stop till it regains 98.10
Keep 98.10; the stop stays
questions.why: 96.10. A gap through the stop hands it to the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day, and the low of that first bar is the new stop. The old stop was jumped, so it no longer says anything. There is a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. Here the loss at 96.10 is a little under 2R, so 96.10 stands.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Sell at the open, 96.50: The gap rule gives it the first 30 minutes. The open is not the decision.
wrong.No stop till it regains 98.10: There is always a stop. The new one is the 30-minute low.
wrong.Keep 98.10; the stop stays: A stop only moves up, but a gap through it is the one exception. The old stop was gapped through, so the first 30 minutes decide.

questions.story: You bought the hold at 100.20 with the stop at 98.10. It opens at 96.50 on a sector headline. The first 30-minute bar's low is 96.10.
questions.simple: It is 96.10, because the old stop was jumped and the first 30 minutes show where the stock settles.

deeper.trap: The ceiling. The new stop only works while the loss at it stays inside 2R. Here it does, narrowly. A first-30-minute low a little lower would put the loss past 2R, and then you get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B20
the 2R ceiling is a computed test, narrowly inside

questions.q: Where may the stop go now?
choices: Up to the entry, breakeven
Lower, to give it more room
A close under the 20 EMA
Remove it; the trade is free
questions.why: Up to the entry. The rulebook moves the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally, so at 3R it may go to the entry. Breakeven is the point after which a trade must never again become a loser. A stop only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: At 3R the stop may move up to the entry. Never down or wider.

wrong.A close under the 20 EMA: A close under a line cannot sit with the broker as an order. Every position keeps a real stop order.
wrong.Lower, to give it more room: A stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Remove it; the trade is free: Every position keeps a real stop order with the broker. Selling some does not remove it.

questions.story: Bought at 183.72 with the stop at 179.97. Within two sessions it reaches 3R.
questions.simple: The stop may go up to the entry, so a trade that reached 3R can no longer turn into a loser.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h05)
rests on the owner's rulebook B19, where breakeven is 'ideally' 2R to 5R

questions.q: The app's market filter (Green, Yellow, Orange, Red) reads Yellow. What does that do to this setup?
choices: Smaller risk, fewer positions
Full risk, the same as in Green
Only the A+ setups get taken
No new longs while it lasts
questions.why: Smaller risk and fewer positions. The market filter is the app's reading of how healthy the market is, and its color says how much the account trades. Green is full risk per grade and up to 10 positions. Yellow is smaller and fewer, because a less healthy market makes any setup less sure. It is a guide.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the line. Yellow trims the size and the count.

wrong.Only the A+ setups get taken: That is a tighter reading than Yellow. Yellow is smaller and fewer, not A+ only.
wrong.No new longs while it lasts: Yellow still trades, smaller and fewer. It does not stop longs.
wrong.Full risk, the same as in Green: That is Green. Yellow cuts size and the number of positions.

questions.simple: Yellow means a less sure market, so we take smaller risk and fewer positions than in Green.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h26)
rests on the owner's rulebook F65, a guide under A10

questions.q: Can you buy it?
choices: Yes; a new trade on a new hold
No; only one try per pullback
No; wait a week after a stop-out
Yes; but only a half-size pilot
questions.answer: Yes; a new trade on a new hold
questions.why: Yes. After a stop-out you buy again only if the setup triggers again. It is a new trade with its own stop and every rule. A stop-out is not a verdict on the setup, so there is no waiting week. A new hold session counts. Tries on one stock are capped by the week and the month.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a verdict on the setup. The next hold is a new trade.

wrong.No; wait a week after a stop-out: The rulebook asks for a new trigger, not a wait. A new hold session is where one starts.
wrong.No; only one try per pullback: The rulebook caps tries by the week and the month, not at one per pullback.
wrong.Yes; but only a half-size pilot: The pullback is a new trade at full size, at one price with one stop. There is no pilot.

questions.story: Your hold buy stopped out on Tuesday, your first try this week. On Thursday the stock again meets every setup test: a fresh dip, a rising line, and a new session that holds it.
questions.simple: Yes, because a fresh hold session is a new trade with its own trigger and stop, and one stop-out does not bar it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B21 and E56
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: On a 20 EMA pullback, our first sell is a judgment, and we rarely make it before day 3.
questions.why: True. The first sell is a judgment that depends on a variety of factors, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. The gain in a pullback buy comes from a push over several days, so we sell into that strength, not first thing.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
questions.simple: True, because the gain comes from a push over several days, so we sell into it, not on day 1.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E51
the levels are adjustable

questions.q: Two six-day pullbacks to the 20 EMA. Which one does Brian Shannon prefer?
choices: The lighter-volume one; less selling
The heavy one; buyers will show
Equal; the touch is the touch
Neither; he ignores volume
questions.why: The quiet drift. Shannon looks for volume contracting during pullbacks, and TraderLion calls a slow drift into the EMAs ideal. Heavy selling into the line is sellers showing. Grading stays a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet into the line is the better sign. Loud into the line is a warning.

wrong.The heavy one; buyers will show: Heavy red days into the line are sellers showing, not buyers. Shannon wants volume to contract on a pullback.
wrong.Equal; the touch is the touch: The touch is the pattern. How price got there matters to him: he looks for contracting volume.
wrong.Neither; he ignores volume: He does not. Shannon looks for volume contracting during pullbacks.

questions.story: Two six-day pullbacks to the 20 EMA. One drifts down on 0.7x volume with small bars. The other has two heavy red days into the line.
questions.simple: The quiet one, because light selling looks like a rest, while heavy selling into the line looks like sellers.

reasons: grading on volume is held under D-006, as a grade cue not a gate

questions.q: What is it?
choices: A lost line; not a pullback
A 20 EMA pullback with a shakeout
A Remount of the 50-day line
A buyable dip; it closed back up
questions.answer: A lost line; not a pullback
questions.why: A lost line. Sellers won the 20 EMA on three of the five closes, so the line was not acting as support. One dip under that comes right back is a shakeout. Three closes under is a line lost, and the setup is off until it sets up again. How far is too far is a judgment call, but three of five is past it. AAPL showed this in January 2022.
questions.lesson_line: Count the closes under the line. One is a shakeout; three is a line lost.

wrong.A 20 EMA pullback with a shakeout: One dip under the line that comes right back is a shakeout. Three closes under is more than that.
wrong.A Remount of the 50-day line: A Remount follows a 50-day line lost for many days in a row. Here the line is the 20 EMA.
wrong.A buyable dip; it closed back up: A close back above does not undo the damage. Three closes under mean sellers won the line on most days.

questions.story: In a five-session pullback the stock closed under its 20 EMA on three of the days. Today it closed back above the line.
questions.simple: It is a lost line, because three closes under the 20 EMA mean sellers won it, not buyers.

deeper.trap: A close back above the line after the damage looks like a recovery, but sellers already won it on most days. Three closes under the 20 EMA ended AAPL's setup in January 2022 before any trigger.

reasons: proposed numbers: one close, 0.5 ATR, two in a row
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Take the pullback?
choices: No; it fails the liquidity rules
No; a four-day pullback is too short
Yes; a clean pattern is the pattern
Yes; the 1% volume cap handles it
questions.answer: No; it fails the liquidity rules
questions.why: No. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one is $7 and about $5 million, so it fails both tests. A thin stock is hard to sell fast, and a stop can slip a long way. Illiquid stocks are not even watched. Bonde: buying such pullbacks on most small caps would make you a bag holder.
questions.lesson_line: A clean tap on a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.Yes; a clean pattern is the pattern: The pattern is fine and the stock is not ours. The liquidity rule comes before the chart.
wrong.No; a four-day pullback is too short: A four-day pullback is a normal length here. The stock fails on price and daily trading, not on length.
wrong.Yes; the 1% volume cap handles it: The volume cap limits what we own in a stock we already trade. It does not make a $7 stock trading about $5 million a day one of ours.

questions.story: A tidy four-day drift to the 20 EMA on a $7 stock that trades about $5 million a day.
questions.simple: No, because a thin stock is hard to sell fast, so we skip it however clean the chart looks.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B23

questions.q: What do you do, and what was the tell?
choices: Stopped out; a late tap of a tired line
Hold; it will remount the line
Widen the stop to the 50-day
questions.answer: Stopped out; a late tap of a tired line
questions.why: Stopped out, by the order. The tell was the 20 EMA already flattening after a four-month run; a flattening line is off before the trigger. NVDA then sat under its 20 EMA for weeks.
questions.lesson_line: Late in a run the line flattens and the taps stop holding. Pass them.

wrong.Hold; it will remount the line: The stop is the exit. Hoping for a remount is how a small loss becomes a big one.
wrong.Widen the stop to the 50-day: The stop only moves up, never wider.

questions.story: Late in a four-month run you bought a tap of the 20 EMA at 181.91, stop 178.01. Next day the low hits 175.49 and the stock closes under the line.

questions.q: By our rule, a long 8% above its 9 EMA is too stretched to buy.
questions.why: False. The rulebook skips a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA. At 8% it passes this test. A stock far above its short average has run fast, and chasing it is not the same as buying a pullback. AlphaTrends says buying strength after a controlled pullback is very different from chasing price after an extended rally. Other rules, such as the 4% no-chase line, still apply.
questions.lesson_line: The stretch line is 10% above the 9 EMA. A run that far tends to rest first.
questions.simple: False, because 8% is not stretched enough to skip, and the line exists so we do not chase a fast run.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h13)
rests on the owner's rulebook C29
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Bought at 28.79, stop 28.02. The stock trades to 32.64. How many R is that?
questions.why: The gain is the exit minus the fill, 32.64 minus 28.79. One R is the fill minus the stop, 28.79 minus 28.02. The gain divided by one R is 5. That is a mark on the ruler, and a later sell is a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. 5R is a mark on the ruler, not a fixed sale.
questions.simple: It is 5R, because the gain is five times the distance from the fill to the stop.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook E51, which is adjustable

wrong.6.0R: That counts the gain from the stop, so it reads one R too high.
wrong.13.4R: That is the percent gain read as R. Divide by the risk instead.
wrong.50.0R: That is ten times too big. A decimal slip.

questions.story: Bought at the trigger.

questions.q: What do you do with the shares you still hold?
choices: Sell a big part into the run
Sell only a small slice
Hold all; the trend is up
Add more; it is strong
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the run
questions.why: Sell a big part into the run. A climax run is a burst of buying at the end of a move: here a third up day, a gap up and the heaviest volume of the run. It is the easiest moment to turn a big gain into cash while buyers are eager. The rulebook says to sell a big part into a climax run on your own long. It is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: When your winner goes vertical, sell them what they want.

wrong.Sell only a small slice: The rule says to sell a big part into the run, not a small slice.
wrong.Hold all; the trend is up: The rule for a climax run on your own long is to sell a big part into it. Holding it all skips that.
wrong.Add more; it is strong: The pullback buy is one price at full size, with no adding. A climax is where we sell, not add.

questions.story: Your pullback buy is up 9R in two weeks. Today is its third straight up day, a gap up on the heaviest volume of the run.
questions.simple: We sell a big part into a climax run, because that is when a big gain is easiest to bank.

deeper.trap: A climax run feels like proof the trade is great, so holding it all feels right. The rule says to sell a big part into it. It is a judgment call, so the exact size is yours, but the call is to sell.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h16)
rests on the owner's rulebook C34, a judgment call

questions.q: A stock opens at 5.4R, past the 5R level you planned to sell at. Our rule makes you sell at the open.
questions.why: False. A gap up past a profit level at the open is not an automatic sell. Selling part at the open is an optional judgment, never a rule. A stock that opens strong can keep running, so we decide by how it trades, not by a fixed level.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past a profit level is not an automatic sale. Selling into it is a judgment.
questions.simple: False, because a strong open can keep running, so selling into a gap is our choice, not a rule.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h25)
rests on the owner's rulebook F63

questions.q: Where does the stop go?
choices: A few cents under 93.60
At the entry price itself
A close under the 20 EMA
A fixed 1% under the entry
questions.why: A few cents under 93.60, the low of day. If the stock trades under today's low after we bought, the dip we bought has failed, so that is where we leave. Our stop goes under the low of day, the prior day's low, or the range low, and the low of day is the main one. The hold candle's low is 93.88, but the next session dipped to 93.60 first.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sits a few cents under the low of day.

wrong.At the entry price itself: A stop right on the entry gives the trade no room. Breakeven comes later, after the trade has worked.
wrong.A close under the 20 EMA: A close under the line is not the first stop. The stop is an order a few cents under a low.
wrong.A fixed 1% under the entry: The stop comes from a low, not from a fixed percent. The size is then set from that stop.

questions.story: The holding candle's low is 93.88. The next session dips to 93.60, still above the rising 20 EMA, then trades over the hold candle's high and you buy.
questions.simple: A few cents under 93.60, because a break of today's low means the dip we bought has failed.

questions.q: Price holds the 20 EMA and the same session closes back over the 9 EMA. On our card, that 9 EMA remount is what?
choices: A confirming sign of the hold
The buy order's trigger
An invalidation of the hold
The line the stop sits at
questions.answer: A confirming sign of the hold
questions.why: A confirming sign, not a gate. On our card a close back over the 9 EMA backs up the hold. It is not the trigger, and a missing remount does not cancel the hold.
questions.lesson_line: The 9 EMA remount backs up the hold. It is not the buy.

wrong.The buy order's trigger: The Model Book playbook makes it the buy. Our card makes it a confirming sign, and the buy is the trade over the hold candle's high.
wrong.An invalidation of the hold: The card calls it a confirming sign. It does not cancel the hold.
wrong.The line the stop sits at: The stop is a few cents under the hold session's low, never a line.

questions.simple: It is a confirming sign, not a gate, so the trade can go on without it.

fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Growing sales and earnings come first in grading a pullback buy; the chart is the tie-breaker.
questions.why: False. The rulebook prefers stocks with growing sales and earnings, but the chart comes first. The chart gives the entry, the stop and the size, which growth alone cannot. Growth is a preference, not a requirement.
questions.lesson_line: Numbers help. The chart decides.
questions.simple: False, because the chart gives the entry and the stop, so it comes first and growth is only a preference.

rests on the owner's rulebook D40

questions.q: Which name fits?
choices: EMA Crossback; a fresh reclaim
20 EMA pullback; old uptrend
Remount; the 50-day was lost
Flag; a pause after a sharp run
questions.why: The EMA Crossback. The stock just turned up out of a decline, and this is its first test of the averages. That is Kell's crossback, taught in its own lesson. Our 20 EMA pullback is for a leader already in an established uptrend.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions since the reclaim. A first test soon after it is a crossback.

wrong.20 EMA pullback; old uptrend: Same line, but the averages were just reclaimed. That makes this first test the EMA Crossback.
wrong.Remount; the 50-day was lost: A Remount retakes a 50-day line lost for many days. This story reclaims the 9 and 20 EMA.
wrong.Flag; a pause after a sharp run: A flag follows a sharp run up. This story is a reclaim of the averages, not a run.

questions.story: The stock slid for weeks, then closed back over its 9 and 20 EMA a few sessions ago. Now it tests the 20 EMA for the first time since.
questions.simple: It is the crossback, because the stock just turned up from a decline, while a pullback is a rest in an old uptrend.

deeper.trap: Both setups touch the same 20 EMA, so the chart can look alike. The tell is the order of events. Here the stock closed back over the 9 and 20 EMA a few sessions ago and this is the first test. Ask when the line was reclaimed before you name the setup.

reasons: rests on D-002 and D-026 defaults
the card's session window is proposed and the Kell quote could not be fetched directly
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Which name fits?
choices: A Remount; a lost line retaken
A 20 EMA pullback, then a bounce
An undercut and rally of a line
An EMA Crossback; the first retest
questions.answer: A Remount; a lost line retaken
questions.why: A Remount. Five or more consecutive closes under a 50-day or 200-day line is a line lost. The close back above it is the retake. Nine closes in a row fits. A pullback allows at most one close under its line.
questions.lesson_line: Count the closes under the line. Five or more in a row, then back above it, is a Remount, not a pullback.

wrong.A 20 EMA pullback, then a bounce: A pullback allows at most one close under its line. This stock lost its 50-day for nine sessions.
wrong.An undercut and rally of a line: Nine closes in a row under the line is five or more, which the card calls a Remount.
wrong.An EMA Crossback; the first retest: A Crossback is the first retest of the averages after the stock has closed back above them. Today is the retake itself, not a retest.

questions.story: The stock closed under its 50-day for nine sessions in a row, then today closed back above it.
questions.simple: It is a Remount, because the stock lost its 50-day for many days in a row and then took it back.

deeper.trap: Counting closes under the wrong line. A pullback allows at most one close under the 20 EMA. A Remount is five or more closes in a row under a 50-day or 200-day line, then retaken. Two closes in a row under the 20 EMA already end the pullback setup, long before it could be a Remount.

reasons: the five-close count is a proposed card number

questions.q: Which name fits, and what decides it?
choices: Bull flag; the pole decides
20 EMA pullback; the line decides
EMA Crossback; the pop decides
No flag; the pole is under 30%
questions.why: A bull flag. A flag needs a pole, a gain of 20% or more inside 20 sessions, then a tight drift. This stock gained 24% in 12 sessions, then moved sideways five days. A 20 EMA pullback needs a session that tags the line, and this range sits well above it.
questions.lesson_line: A pole in front of a tight drift makes a flag. A pullback needs a session that tags the line.

wrong.20 EMA pullback; the line decides: A pullback needs a session whose low tags the line. This range sits well above it, and a pole stands in front. That is a flag.
wrong.EMA Crossback; the pop decides: A crossback follows a reclaim of the averages out of a decline. The story describes a 24% rise, not a reclaim.
wrong.No flag; the pole is under 30%: Kullamagi's 30% to 100% or more is the prior move for his own breakout setup. Our flag card needs a pole of 20% or more inside 20 sessions.

questions.story: The stock rose 24% in 12 sessions, then moved sideways in a tight range for five days. Its 20 EMA is still well below the range.
questions.simple: It is a bull flag, because the 24% rise in 12 sessions is a pole followed by a tight drift.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi wants a move of 30% to 100% or more before his own breakout setup. That is his filter, not our flag card, which needs a gain of 20% or more inside 20 sessions. Do not carry one number into the other's rule.

reasons: tied to held decision D-029
the 20% in 20 sessions pole is a proposed number
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Which name fits?
choices: The MAU&R costume of U&R
The 20 EMA pullback setup
A Remount of the lost line
No trade; any break kills it
questions.why: The undercut and rally in its moving-average costume. Ask what the buy is. On our current default, a low that undercut the 20 EMA, bought as the move back above the line, is the U&R. The pullback buys the intraday turn off a held line.
questions.lesson_line: Same line, different buy. Buying the move back through the line is the U&R, not the pullback.

wrong.The 20 EMA pullback setup: Its buy is the turn off a held line, such as red to green. Buying the move back above the line is the U&R.
wrong.A Remount of the lost line: The line was under water for two hours, not for five or more closes. That is an undercut, not a lost line.
wrong.No trade; any break kills it: The rules that end a setup count closes under the line, not intraday breaks. This buy is a different setup, the U&R.

questions.story: At 10 am the low breaks 1% under the 20 EMA. By noon price is back above the line and you buy the move back through it.
questions.simple: It is the undercut and rally, because the buy came as price moved back through the line.

deeper.trap: The same chart can be two setups. A shallow undercut can sit inside the pullback's touch band, so depth alone cannot name it. The buy names it. Buy the intraday turn off a held low and it is the pullback. Buy the move back through the line and it is the U&R.

reasons: rests on held decisions D-002, D-003 and D-036
keyed on provisional defaults that may change
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Are these 20 EMA pullbacks?
choices: No; not longs under the 200-day
Yes; the 20 EMA held both times
Yes, but at half the usual size
No; two holds in a month is too few
questions.why: No. We take no longs below the 200-day simple moving average unless it is a parabolic long. Both bounces happened under a falling 200-day, so they are bear-market bounces, not pullbacks in a trend. AlphaTrends puts it the other way: above the 200-day, the larger trend is innocent until proven guilty.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day a hold of the 20 EMA is a bounce. We do not buy bounces.

wrong.Yes; the 20 EMA held both times: The holds are real and the context is wrong. The 200-day rule is a hard line.
wrong.Yes, but at half the usual size: Size does not fix the context. No longs below the 200-day unless it is a parabolic long.
wrong.No; two holds in a month is too few: The count of holds is not the test. The test is the larger trend: no longs below the 200-day unless it is a parabolic long.

questions.story: In a bear market a stock bounces off its 20 EMA twice in a month. Both times price is under a falling 200-day.
questions.simple: No, because we do not buy longs below the 200-day, so a hold of the 20 EMA there is only a bounce.

deeper.trap: Two clean holds of the 20 EMA feel like proof. Under a falling 200-day they are bounces. The rule is no longs below the 200-day simple moving average unless it is a parabolic long, so check the 200-day before the 20 EMA.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h10)
rests on the owner's rulebook B26
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: On our card, a stock above a 200-day that is lower than it was 20 sessions earlier still passes the context.
questions.why: False. The card's context line says the 200-day SMA is not lower than it was 20 sessions earlier. A 200-day that is lower fails it, even with price above it. A flat 200-day passes.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, and the 200-day not lower than 20 sessions ago. Both halves matter.
questions.simple: False, because the card wants the 200-day to be no lower than it was 20 sessions earlier.

deeper.counter: Above the 200-day is the rulebook line. The slope test is the card's own extra. A stock above a 200-day that is lower than 20 sessions ago passes the rulebook line but fails the card's context.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c08)
the 20 session slope test is a proposed number
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Is it still a valid setup? Our grade (A+ to B-) says how clean a setup is and sets the size.
choices: Yes; the volume lowers its grade
No; heavy selling voids the setup
Yes; the volume makes no difference
No; wait for volume to dry up first
questions.answer: Yes; the volume lowers its grade
questions.why: Yes, at a lower grade. A heavy-volume down day into the line is a distribution day: a warning to be mindful of, not an invalidation. The hold closed above the line, so buyers still defended it. A lower grade can mean a smaller size, so the setup stays and we may risk less. INTC had one in November 2017.
questions.lesson_line: One loud red day into the line is a warning and a lower grade. It does not void the setup.

wrong.No; heavy selling voids the setup: It lowers the grade. It does not void the setup.
wrong.Yes; the volume makes no difference: Volume does move the grade. Heavy selling into the line is a warning and a lower grade.
wrong.No; wait for volume to dry up first: Volume is not a requirement for the setup to count. The hold has happened, so the heavy day only lowers the grade.

questions.story: The hold session. A pullback to the 20 EMA holds and closes above the line. One of its down days ran on 2.3x the 50-day volume.
questions.simple: Yes, at a lower grade, because heavy selling is a warning, and a lower grade can mean a smaller size.

deeper.trap: The loud red day is easy to read as a veto. Our rule: a heavy down day is a warning and a lower grade, never an invalidation. Do not wave it through either. Grade it down. INTC in 2017 had one on 2.3 times.

reasons: rests on the settled HEAVY-DOWN ruling (2026-11-14)
the 1.5x line is a card number

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Our limit on one stock is at most ___ tries in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.why: 3. At most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. Each try is a new trade on a new hold session, with its own trigger and stop.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week and six a month on one stock. That is the cap.
questions.simple: The most is 3 tries a week on one stock, and 6 in a month.

deeper.trap: The cap counts every try on one stock, and each try must be a new trade with its own trigger and stop. A stop-out is not a reason to skip the cap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E56
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Was the loss a mistake?
choices: No; the stop did its job here
No; the close back up erased the loss
Yes; re-buy at 546.88 and hold
Yes; a stop-out means a bad setup
questions.answer: No; the stop did its job here
questions.why: No. The stop is the exit, and it did its job when the low of 538.05 ran through 540.97. We size so a stop-out is a small loss we planned for, and a stock that runs after we are out does not make the exit wrong. A re-buy at the old price is not a rule: after a stop-out we buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade. CAT reached 610 without us, and that is the cost of taking the exit.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working, even when the stock runs after.

wrong.Yes; re-buy at 546.88 and hold: After a stop-out you buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade. A chase back in is not a trigger.
wrong.Yes; a stop-out means a bad setup: A stop-out does not make a setup bad. Judge the trade by the plan, not by what the stock does next. The stop is the exit, and taking it is the plan.
wrong.No; the close back up erased the loss: The stop fired when the low traded through 540.97. A later close above it does not undo the exit.

questions.story: You bought a hold at 558.32 with the stop at 540.97, about 3.1% wide. Next day the stock opens at 543.35, still above the stop, then the low prints 538.05 and the stop fires. It closes 546.88 and reaches 610 within a month.
questions.simple: No, because the stop did its job, and a stock running after you are out does not make the exit wrong.

deeper.trap: Judging the trade by what came after. CAT closed at 546.88 and reached 610 within a month, but nobody knew that at the low of 538.05. A stop cannot know what comes next, so it is judged by the plan, not by the aftermath.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B21 and A4
3.1% stop width is held under D-005
one worked example

questions.q: Hold through the report?
choices: No; hold through only if up 5R
No; the 3-day window bars holding it
Yes; it is nearly at the 5R line
Yes; a breakeven stop protects it
questions.answer: No; hold through only if up 5R
questions.why: No. We hold through an earnings report only if the trade is up 5R, and 3.9R at the peak is not 5R. A report can gap the stock past the stop, so we hold only when the gain is big enough to cushion that. The rule also bars new buys in the 3 days before a report. NVDA in May 2023 peaked at 3.9R before its report, so the rule had us out before the gap.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you cannot stop. Five R buys the ticket; almost does not.

wrong.Yes; it is nearly at the 5R line: Almost is under the line. The rule is 5R, not nearly 5R.
wrong.No; the 3-day window bars holding it: The 3-day window bars new buys, not holding. What decides holding is the 5R test, and 3.9R is short of it.
wrong.Yes; a breakeven stop protects it: A stop is an order, not a guarantee against a gap. The rule is to hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.

questions.story: Your 20 EMA pullback buy has never passed 3.9R, and the company reports tomorrow.
questions.simple: No, because a report can gap the stock past the stop, and 3.9R is not a big enough cushion.

deeper.counter: This rule costs upside. NVDA's best run in our data was 25.1R, and the rule had us out under 5R before the report. We accept that cost to avoid a gap past the stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B22

questions.q: The trigger is 45.00 and the stock opens at 46.62, above it. How far above the trigger is the open, in percent?
questions.why: The open's gain over the trigger is (46.62 minus 45.00) divided by 45.00, which is 3.6%. That is inside the 4% line, so the fill at the open is allowed. The stop stays under the hold candle, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap against the trigger. Inside 4% you may take the open.
questions.simple: The open is 3.6% above the trigger, which is under the 4% limit, so we may take the open.

deeper.trap: Inside 4% does not mean a free trade. The stop stays under the hold candle, so a higher fill widens the stop distance and the shares shrink. At 3.6% above the trigger the size is already smaller than planned.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook C28

wrong.103.6%: That is the open as a share of the trigger, not the gain.
wrong.162.0%: Turned the dollar gap into a percent without dividing by the trigger.

questions.q: What happens to the last third?
choices: Sold on the close under it
Held; the stop is at breakeven
Added to, buying the dip
Held to a fixed 8R target
questions.answer: Sold on the close under it
questions.why: Sold. Two thirds are banked at 3R and 5R. The last third trails the 10-day line for a fast mover or the 21-day for a steadier one. A close below the line is the exit.
questions.lesson_line: Two thirds banked, the last third on the trail. The close below the line is the exit.

wrong.Held; the stop is at breakeven: Breakeven is the floor, not the plan. The trail is the exit for the last third.
wrong.Added to, buying the dip: Full size at one price; no adding. A close under the trail is an exit, not an add.
wrong.Held to a fixed 8R target: The last third trails the line. There is no fixed target.

questions.story: You bought ILMN's hold at 95.90, stop 93.85. 3R came in 10 sessions and a third came off; 5R and another third. ILMN is a steady mover, so you trail its 21-day. Weeks later it closes under that line.
questions.simple: The last third is sold, because the stock closed under its 21-day trail line.

deeper.counter: Breakeven is only the floor under the last third. The trail is the plan: the 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones, sold on a close below it. ILMN's best run reached 40.2R, so a fixed target of 8R would have sold far too soon.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E51 and E52
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: A 20 EMA that crosses under the 50-day SMA before the trigger ends the pullback setup.
questions.why: True. A 20 EMA that crosses under the 50-day SMA breaks the proper order of the trend averages, so this is a stock in repair, not a leader resting. A 20 EMA that flattens or turns down says the same. The setup is off before entry. Keller's proper order has the fast EMA over the 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: The fast line under the slow line is not a pullback. It is a trend in trouble.
questions.simple: True, because a 20 EMA under the 50-day means the trend is weakening, so this is no leader resting.

deeper.trap: The test is before the trigger. A cross that happens after you are in is a different decision. The stop and the trail manage the exit, not this entry test.

reasons: the cross test is a proposed card line

questions.q: What is the right fix?
choices: Stop under the low; size from it
Keep the close stop; resize for 4%
A real 1.5% stop; keep the size
Keep both; the line is a fine stop
questions.answer: Stop under the low; size from it
questions.why: Stop under the low, then the size from it. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, and a close under a line cannot sit there as an order. Sizing for a 1.5% stop when the real one is 4% away means one loss costs far more than planned. Set the stop first, then size from it. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: A line is not an order, and a size is never chosen before the stop.

wrong.Keep the close stop; resize for 4%: Resizing helps, but a close under a line cannot sit with the broker as an order. The stop is still not real.
wrong.A real 1.5% stop; keep the size: The stop comes from the chart, not from the size you want. Stop first, then the size from it, or skip the trade.
wrong.Keep both; the line is a fine stop: A line is a place to watch. The stop is a price with the broker, a few cents under the hold session's low.

questions.story: A member sets the stop as a close under the 20 EMA, about 4% away. The member sizes the position as if the stop were 1.5% away.
questions.simple: Put a real stop order under the hold low, then size from it, so a loss never costs more than planned.

deeper.trap: Sizing off the stop you wish you had. The size comes from the real exit. With the real exit 4% away, a size built for 1.5% risks far more than planned. The fix is a stop a few cents under the hold session's low, then the size from it, or skip the trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3, A5 and D41

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, earliest sell.
choices: Market 100.39; stop 99.07; sell day 3+
Limit on the 20 EMA; stop 95.00; hold
Market at the close; stop 50-day; day 1
Market 100.38; stop 99.10; all out at 5R
questions.why: Market at 100.39, as price trades a cent over the hold candle's high of 100.38. The stop goes a few cents under the hold low of 99.10, which is 99.07, so the risk stays small. The first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 at the earliest, because the gain comes from a push over several days. GE reached 3R in 5 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, first sell, trail. Write it before the open; execute it without a debate.

wrong.Limit on the 20 EMA; stop 95.00; hold: A limit on the line buys before a hold, and a stop at 95.00 is nowhere near the hold candle's low.
wrong.Market 100.38; stop 99.10; all out at 5R: The buy is a cent over the hold high, not at it. The stop sits a few cents under the low, not on it. And the first sell is a judgment, not an all-out sale at 5R.
wrong.Market at the close; stop 50-day; day 1: The trigger is the trade over the hold candle's high, not the close, and the 50-day is not a stop. We very rarely sell on day 1.

questions.story: The hold session. It holds the rising 20 EMA and closes above it. Its low is 99.10 and its high is 100.38.
questions.simple: Buy as price pushes over the hold high, stop just under its low to keep risk small, and sell no earlier than day 3.

deeper.example: GE, January 2024: the low kissed the line to the cent, a 1.3% stop, and the stock reached 3R in 5 sessions. The stop may move up to breakeven as the trade works. The first sell is a judgment.

reasons: the buy is the proposed fallback trigger, held under D-003
rests on the owner's rulebook
